Eric, we looked at the horizontal-table -> vertical-chunk rewrite question.

Short version: I don’t think we should pipeline the rewrite through the GPU as a standalone step. The direct C++ engine surface is already column-native, so no engine/API change is needed. If libbitcoin keeps horizontal mmap storage, the rotation is a storage-layer staging cost, not an engine integration issue.

Local microbench numbers on this machine:

- ECDSA CPU full AoS->SoA rewrite: ~22.9 GB/s, about 39s projected over 3.5B tuples.
- Best CPU chunk size was ~1024 rows: ~29.1 GB/s, about 31s projected over 3.5B tuples.
- Schnorr was similar: ~30s projected at best chunk size.
- Multithreading did not help; throughput stayed around ~20-23 GB/s, so one core is basically saturating the write path.
- GPU staging on RTX 5060 Ti was PCIe-bound: pinned H2D ~19.9 GB/s, and H2D + deinterleave kernel projected around ~40s.

So my recommendation is:

1. Keep the direct column API as the engine boundary.
2. If storage stays horizontal, do CPU chunk rotation, preferably fused with the existing read/staging path and overlapped with verification.
3. Don’t offload only the row->column rewrite to GPU; the PCIe transfer cost removes the benefit.
4. Treat vertical mmap aggregation as an end-to-end libbitcoin storage experiment. It may still win if the mmap aggregation change eliminates the contention you’re seeing, but the engine does not need a different interface for that.

No C ABI, shim, or bridge is needed for this path.

And there is an accessor that allows the stream read/write in logical tables to obtain the offset pointer the specific columns. So that is buried in the existing logical table wrapper object for the vertical tables, so that the columns are sub-named. Agreed. We should keep consensus verdicts and engine/operational failures strictly separate.

If verification completes, then a row can be valid or consensus-invalid. But if the engine cannot complete the operation due to GPU allocation, launch/copy failure, unsupported backend, cancellation, or an internal invariant failure, that must be reported as an operational error, not as “all signatures invalid”.

For the direct libbitcoin integration we are moving toward a C++ status/result contract for the GPU/batch paths, so libbitcoin can decide whether to retry on CPU, abort cleanly, or shut down. The direct path will not go through the C ABI/bridge, but the same distinction will exist internally through GpuError/status propagation.

After initially optimizing the full vertical table implementation for minimal locking (1 vs 4 per composite 4 column table), and eliminating all allocations during multisig capture, I found that there was still a significant performance issue. Eventually I was able to determine that this was chaotic behavior not caused by any single inefficiency (like table allocator `locks` or `copy` and `malloc` excess) but instead by insufficient control over batch sizes.

The config sets a minimum batch size, and then the node cuts off the capture in the validation message pipeline. However because a full window worth of block validations (e.g. 50k blocks) can pass that gate almost immediately, being queued up for concurrent validate, the result is a pressure wave that eventually cuts out all batch draining until the window closes. This dramatically oversized the batch tables creating a large amount of I/O back pressure.

This was exacerbated by an oversight in the calculation of the window itself when batching, as using the `prevalid` state (validated and batch accumulated, but sigs not yet verified) *and* the `valid` state (post-verify) led to a doubling of the intended window size. After resolving this so that it maintains the window only on the `valid` state, performance was materially improved. But the major issue of excessive table sizing remained.

Prior to optimizing above, the full validation run bypassing sig verify took about `6:00`. After the above changes that was down to around `4:00`. Then made the change to increase control over table excesses, but moving the batch cutoff out of the ASIO message pump and into the executing validations. At the same time I removed the reader-writer mutex lock that was set up to guard the batch tables during verify, replaced with an atomic turnstile. This reduced the above total time to `3:18` as it brought batch tables into a very well-controlled range (1.0 - 1.2x of target).

However the turnstile was set up to allow blocks to continue to validate (unbatched, with inline sig verify) when the batch cutoff was signaled. This allowed about 24% of all batchable signatures to bypass capture. That's about 43 minutes of pure sig verify cost. This is far greater than optimal, so I've modified the turnstile to allow blocks to write into the batch cutoff, while still allowing them to validate inline during the batch verify. It may turn out that validating during GPU verify is also suboptimal, as pre and post-processing the GPU may be slowed by it, in which case that can be adjusted as well.

Claude summarizing why POSIX operating systems are fundamentally broken, tracing it back to a consequence of process forking...

"
fork() is the root cause.Forking a process nominally requires duplicating its entire address space. COW makes that affordable only if the kernel

memory it doesn't have — strict accounting would make fork of any large process fail outright (a 400GB process would need 400GB of headroom to fork a shell). So POSIX institutionalized overcommit to keep its own primitive viable.

Overcommit converts allocation failure into asynchronous process termination.The kernel's promises come due at page-touch time, when there's no error path to return — so it kills processes (OOM killer, jetsam). Windows, having never carried fork, does strict commit accounting against RAM + pagefile: allocation fails at a decidable point with an error you can handle, and committed memory you actually use just pages — degradation, not death.

The contract violation.An OS multiplexes resources: excess CPU demand yields slowness, never termination. Strict-commit RAM behaves the same way — more demand, more paging, slower. Killing a process because the kernel promised what it didn't have is the OS defaulting on its own accounting and executing the creditor. We agreed fork itself is archaic — posix_spawn and threads cover its legitimate uses — but the overcommit regime it justified persists.

The mmap consequence — the part that bites libbitcoin.Because an overcommitted kernel is perpetually at risk of needing pages it promised elsewhere, it must keep reclaim viable — and dirty file-backed pages can't be reclaimed until cleaned. So POSIX kernels aggressively bound the dirty pool and force writeback early. Linux at least exposes the bound (

et al., system-wide); macOS's UBC hardcodes it with no interface at all. Net result: on a 796GB machine with the RAM bought and paid for, macOS permits roughly 20GB of accumulated dirty mmap before forced writeback throttles the writers — while Windows lets the accumulate-then-flush design work exactly as intended, by default. And the whole regime is futile anyway: the overcommit it protects still breaks eventually; it just chooses when to break someone else's process.

I asked how and when it started, and the lineage is damning...

"About 63 years. The lineage:

1962–63— Melvin Conway (of Conway's Law) described the fork–join concept in his paper "A Multiprocessor System Design," as a notation for splitting computation into parallel paths. That's the origin of the idea and the name.

~1965–66— Project Genie's Berkeley Timesharing System on the SDS 940 implemented fork as an actual system call creating a process copy — Butler Lampson and colleagues. This is the direct ancestor of the Unix semantics.

1969— Thompson carried it into the first Unix on the PDP-7, reportedly in part because copying the process image was one of the easiest ways to implement process creation on that machine: the original fork fit in roughly 27 lines of PDP-7 assembly. No virtual memory, no COW — it literally swapped the process image out and kept both copies.
So the design your 796GB machine is being throttled by was devised for a machine with about 8K words of memory, and chosen substantially because it was

on 1969 hardware — the address-space-duplication semantics weren't a considered design goal so much as an artifact of swapping. Every subsequent complication — COW, overcommit, the OOM killer, untunable dirty-page bounds — is scaffolding erected to keep that 27-line expedient viable as memory grew six orders of magnitude around it.

It's also worth noting the industry has quietly conceded the point: POSIX itself added

(1999), Apple's own frameworks discourage fork-without-exec (Objective-C/Swift runtimes are fork-unsafe by design), and fork doesn't exist on Windows NT, nor in any modern OS research design — Fuchsia's Zircon, for instance, deliberately omitted it. The 2019 HotOS paper "A fork() in the road" (Microsoft Research/BU) makes essentially your argument academically: fork is a terrible abstraction whose costs — overcommit among them — are systemic. The technique outlived its usefulness decades ago; the memory-accounting regime it necessitated is the part that refuses to die."

v145 is required, not preferred — the vc143 package references `__std_rotate`, which exists only in the v145 STL, so it will not link against any v143 toolset.

`Option-ultrafast` defines `WITH_ULTRAFAST` → `HAVE_ULTRAFAST` and sets `Linkage-ultrafast=static`. `Option-cuda` links `secp256k1_gpu_host` + `secp256k1_cuda` + `cudart_static` and adds `/INCLUDE:secp256k1_gpu_columns_provider_anchor`. **Both default to false** — build without them and it compiles clean, links no GPU, and silently runs CPU-only.
